newsitem.title: USA: Bell Atlantic to invest $5 billion in wireline network.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic to invest $5 billion in wireline network.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp., whose $25.6 billion merger with Nynex Corp. was approved Thursday, said Friday it plans to invest $5 billion to upgrade its telephone network as it prepares for a push into the long-distance market.
The company said it aims to capture at least 25 percent of the long-distance market in its region in the next five years.

In a statement marking completion of the merger, Bell Atlantic said it will offer in-region long-distance service "as soon as possible," adding that this could provide $20 billion in sales for the merged company.

The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday approved the merger of Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex, which forms the largest local carrier and No. 2 phone company after AT&T Corp. The company's combined sales will be close to $30 billion.

At a news conference in New York, Bell Atlantic executives said they believe the company has a head start on other Baby Bells to win regulatory approval to offer long-distance phone service in its 12-state local service region.
Bell Atlantic Chairman Raymond Smith said the merged company was "more uniquely positioned to get into long-distance than any of the other companies."

He and other officials said the conditions agreed to with the FCC for approval of the merger gave the company a lead in long-distance. The commitments are meant to lower barriers to competition in Bell Atlantic's local service region stretching from Maine to Virginia. Regulators want such barriers to drop before allowing Baby Bells to offer long-distance services.
"We think they would look favorably" on a regulatory application to enter the long-distance market, one Bell Atlantic executive said, referring to the FCC.
The officials said the company has no plans to use the courts to win entry to the long-distance market, a tactic that SBC Communications Inc. and Ameritech Corp. have pursued.
"We think we will be in long-distance very soon," Smith said.
"The next issues for us (are) to move slowly into video and aggressively into long-distance," said Bell Atlantic Vice President Ivan Seidenberg.
Discussing the executive succession plans for the company, Smith disputed a report that he might have hesitations about carrying through on making Seidenberg his successor.
"I think that there was a misunderstanding," Smith said, referring to a recent Wall Street Journal article. "What I am saying is that there are no guarantees in life."
But he quickly stressed that "Ivan is my candidate. He is the person the board has accepted," Smith said, adding that the Seidenberg's employment agreement was "pretty air-tight."
Smith is scheduled to remain chairman and CEO for a year after the merger is completed. Seidenberg would become CEO by August 1998 and take on the post of chairman after Smith retires.
Bell Atlantic stock fell 25 cents to $75.69 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
